command: ccx discuss --with codex,claude,deepseek --tier T1 --question-file q.txt (temporary CCX_HUB)
question:
A command-line tool writes a small JSON state file that a local web page polls every 2 seconds (the page's server reads the file). The tool must run on Windows, macOS and Linux. Which way of writing the file should it use, and why?
(A) open(path, "w") and json.dump straight into it
(B) write the whole JSON to path + ".tmp" in the same folder, then os.replace(tmp, path)
(C) write to path + ".tmp", then os.rename(tmp, path)
(D) write straight into the file, but take a separate lock file around every write and read
Consider a reader that sees a half-written file, what os.rename does on Windows when the target exists, and a reader or antivirus program that has the file open at the moment of the swap. Give one recommendation and what the reader side should do.

result.recommendation: (B). Serialize the whole JSON, write to a unique same-directory temp file (tempfile.mkstemp), chmod if writer/reader users differ, flush+fsync, close, then os.replace. Retry PermissionError from antivirus/readers about 5 times within 0.5s; if exhausted keep the old file, delete the temp in finally, log failure. Reader: open-parse-close each 2s poll, keep last valid state on OSError/JSONDecodeError, and mark data stale when its timestamp exceeds ~3 poll intervals. Read-only; no files …
consensus: Both sides choose (B): the reader must never see a partially written target, and os.replace is the portable swap; os.rename fails on Windows when the target exists, which rules out (C).
(A) exposes half-written JSON; (D) requires reader and writer to both honour a lock and can leave a stale lock file after a crash.
Reader opens briefly, reads, closes per poll, catches OSError and JSON decode errors, keeps last valid state; writer flushes and fsyncs before replacing.
disagreements: Retry budget: proposer fixed 5 attempts/0.5s; critic says that is unverified against an AV or reader holding the file for seconds — raise the budget or accept dropping the update.
mkstemp default 0600 permissions were never answered by the proposer; critic wants an explicit chmod or a confirmed same-user assumption.
Concurrent writers: critic wants a documented single-writer assumption or a version field to stop timestamp regression; proposer only added unique temp names.
reasons: 5 tries/0.5s keeps the writer bounded inside the page's 2s poll and makes failure observable; dropping one update beats falling back to a direct write.
A timestamp in the JSON plus a staleness threshold above the 2s poll exposes persistent AV blocking to the page without any locking.
